steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper revisiting block-based quantisation for sub-8-bit LLM inference. Explain why LLM quantisation matters (including custom hardware), why activation outliers make it hard, what our variance observations show, and list our contributions.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Pre-trained Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive performance on many Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks. But their computational and memory costs are a critical bottleneck for using them. For example, the larger models in the GPT family have up to hundreds of billions of parameters, and storing these parameters in float16 format needs at least 300GB of memory. Quantisation is a natural way to reduce the cost of running inference on these LLMs, because a low-precision format saves cost on all the relevant efficiency metrics: less on-chip memory, more arithmetic intensity for matrix multiplies, and less DRAM bandwidth needed. Also, services like ChatGPT are becoming more and more popular, which is a reason to explore custom silicon for LLM inference. So the question is: what would a low-precision number system look like in these LLM hardware accelerators (ASICs) of the near future?

Quantising LLMs is challenging because some activations have large absolute magnitudes, which are called activation outliers. Previous approaches proposed different techniques for these outliers. But they either need additional treatments in the integer quantisation domain (LLM.int8() and SmoothQuant) or the performance is not satisfactory (ZeroQuant), and prior work mostly focused on arithmetics that can be ported to GPUs. We observe that because of the outliers, different scaling factors are needed at a finer granularity than per-tensor or per-token level. This leads us to revisit arithmetic systems with small exponents, like MiniFloat, Block Minifloat, Block Logarithm, and Block Floating Point, since they can represent outliers in Transformer models well. As far as we know, our work is the first to systematically investigate short-exponent arithmetics for LLM quantisation.

- Figure 1: variance of tensors joining GEMMs in OPT-6.7B; 128 Wikitext2 samples, float32
  - 1) variance up with depth; 2) some tensors (e.g. \mathbf{K}) larger; 3) weights smaller than activations
  - same in other LLMs; Vicuna-7B plot in Appendix (Figure 4)
- Numerical scaling offsets
  - one config for whole network doesn't work; different ranges/granularities; fine-grained non-linear quantisation
- Table 1 + contributions
  - all GEMMs (8/8); PTQ and TAQ; where to do TAQ and search in NLP pipeline
  - scaling offsets view; block arithmetic framework, nearly-lossless W6A6; 4-bit via fine-tuning and mixed-precision search, ASICs

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Pre-trained Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive performance on many Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks. But their computational and memory costs are a critical bottleneck for using them. For example, the larger models in the GPT family have up to hundreds of billions of parameters, and storing these parameters in float16 format needs at least 300GB of memory. Quantisation is a natural way to reduce the cost of running inference on these LLMs, because a low-precision format saves cost on all the relevant efficiency metrics: less on-chip memory, more arithmetic intensity for matrix multiplies, and less DRAM bandwidth needed. Also, services like ChatGPT are becoming more and more popular, which is a reason to explore custom silicon for LLM inference. So the question is: what would a low-precision number system look like in these LLM hardware accelerators (ASICs) of the near future?

Quantising LLMs is challenging because some activations have large absolute magnitudes, which are called activation outliers. Previous approaches proposed different techniques for these outliers. But they either need additional treatments in the integer quantisation domain (LLM.int8() and SmoothQuant) or the performance is not satisfactory (ZeroQuant), and prior work mostly focused on arithmetics that can be ported to GPUs. We observe that because of the outliers, different scaling factors are needed at a finer granularity than per-tensor or per-token level. This leads us to revisit arithmetic systems with small exponents, like MiniFloat, Block Minifloat, Block Logarithm, and Block Floating Point, since they can represent outliers in Transformer models well. As far as we know, our work is the first to systematically investigate short-exponent arithmetics for LLM quantisation.

Figure 1 shows the variance of the tensors that join the GEMMs in an OPT-6.7B. We fed 128 samples from Wikitext2 to the pretrained float32 model and made three interesting observations. 1) The variance of most activations in Figure 1 gets bigger as the layer gets deeper; 2) Some tensors (e.g. \mathbf{K}) always have a larger variance than the others; 3) All the weight variance is smaller than the activations. Other LLMs show similar trends. There is a variance plot of Vicuna-7B in the Appendix (Figure 4).

Because the numerical ranges vary across layers and tensors, it is hard for a single quantisation configuration to work well for the whole network. From the arithmetic point of view we call this numerical scaling offsets, because quantisation needs different numerical ranges and granularities. For optimal performance these layers should get fine-grained non-linear quantisation strategies.

Table 1 compares our work with existing LLM quantisation methods. Our quantisation covers all GEMMs (8/8) in transformer layers, and both Post-Training-Quantisation (PTQ) and Training-After-Quatisation (TAQ) scenarios. We also look at where in the whole NLP pipeline it makes sense to do TAQ and quantisation search. Our contributions are:

- • We look at the LLM quantisation problem with activation outliers as a scaling offsets problem from the point of view of arithmetic design. We show that a family of arithmetic systems with short exponents shared across a block of numbers works well.

- • We propose a new quantisation framework based on block arithmetic, and show that it works for W6A6 inference on various tasks. Our W6A6 is nearly lossless and is better than prior work in arithmetic density and memory density, and it does not need data calibration or fine-tuning.

- • We present two methods for 4-bit quantisation on downstream tasks: one is based on fine-tuning, and the other one is mixed-precision search. The mixed-precision search also shows the potential advantage of moving LLM inference to cost-effective ASICs.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Pre-trained Large Language Models (LLMs) [1,2,3] have demonstrated impressive performance on a range of Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks. However, their computational and memory costs are a critical bottleneck to their usability. For instance, the larger variants in the GPT family scale up to hundreds of billions of parameters, requiring at least 300GB of memory to store these parameters in float16 format [1]. Quantisation is a natural solution for reducing the cost of running inference on these LLMs [4,5,6], since a low-precision format enables cost savings across all relevant efficiency metrics: reduced on-chip memory, increased arithmetic intensity for matrix multiplies, and decreased DRAM bandwidth requirements. At the same time, the growing popularity of services such as ChatGPT [7] provides an impetus for exploring custom silicon to support LLM inference. This raises the question: what would a low-precision number system look like in these near-future LLM hardware accelerators (ASICs)?

LLM quantisation is challenging because of activations with large absolute magnitudes, also known as activation outliers [8,5]. Previous approaches have proposed various techniques to address such outliers. However, these either require additional treatments in the integer quantisation domain (LLM.int8() and SmoothQuant) or yield unsatisfactory performance (ZeroQuant), and prior work has mainly focused on arithmetics that can be ported to GPUs. We observe that the presence of outliers requires different scaling factors at a finer granularity than the per-tensor or per-token level [4,5]. This insight leads us to revisit arithmetic systems with small exponents, such as MiniFloat [9], Block Minifloat [10], Block Logarithm [11], and Block Floating Point [12], as they can effectively represent outliers in Transformer models. To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first to systematically investigate short-exponent arithmetics for LLM quantisation.

Figure 1 illustrates the variance of the tensors joining the GEMMs in an OPT-6.7B [3]. After feeding 128 samples from Wikitext2 to the pretrained float32 model, we make three interesting observations: 1) the variance of most activations in Figure 1 increases with the depth of the layer; 2) certain tensors (e.g. \mathbf{K}) consistently have a greater variance than others; 3) all the weight variance is smaller than the activations. Similar trends can be observed in other LLMs; we provide a variance plot of Vicuna-7B [15] in the Appendix (Figure 4).

These varying numerical ranges across layers and tensors challenge the efficacy of a single quantisation configuration for the entire network. From an arithmetic perspective, we refer to this phenomenon as numerical scaling offsets, since it requires different numerical ranges and granularities for quantisation. For optimal performance, these layers should be subjected to fine-grained non-linear quantisation strategies.

Table 1 compares our work with existing LLM quantisation methods. Our quantisation considers all GEMMs (8/8) in transformer layers, and both Post-Training-Quantisation (PTQ) and Training-After-Quatisation (TAQ) scenarios. We also explore suitable places within the entire NLP pipeline to perform TAQ and quantisation search. We make the following contributions:

- • We address the LLM quantisation problem with activation outliers and examine it as a scaling offsets problem from an arithmetic design perspective. We demonstrate the efficacy of a family of arithmetic systems with short exponents shared across a block of numbers.

- • We propose a novel quantisation framework based on block arithmetic and demonstrate its effectiveness for W6A6 inference on various tasks. Our nearly-lossless W6A6 outperforms prior work in arithmetic density and memory density, without requiring data calibration or fine-tuning.

- • We present two methods to achieve 4-bit quantisation on downstream tasks: one is fine-tuning-based, and the other is mixed-precision search. The latter further shows the potential advantage of shifting LLM inference to cost-effective ASICs.
